items.title: Global default for Copilot features generally available
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: In September, we announced a global default policy for generally available GitHub Copilot features and supported client capabilities on Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise plans. Starting today, we’re gradually rolling out enforcement of the policy through October 26, so it may take effect at different times for different enterprises and organizations. Eligible features left unconfigured will be set according to the global policy. Administrators can still make explicit choices for individual features at any time. The policy applies to eligible settings on “Features & clients” and “MCP servers in Copilot”. You can review your setting under AI Controls → Copilot → Default policy for new features. For eligibility and exceptions, see the documentation on default availability. What’s changing Once the policy takes effect for your enterprise or organization: Eligible generally available features and capabilities left Unconfigured will be set according to the selected global default of Enabled, Disabled, or Let organizations decide. This is a one-time change. Subsequent changes to the default policy won’t change feature policies that are already set. Explicit choices are preserved. If you’ve enabled or disabled an individual feature, the rollout won’t change that setting. Preview features remain opt-in. If you opted into a preview that later becomes generally available, your choice will be preserved. Otherwise, the default policy will apply when it becomes eligible. Join the discussion within GitHub Community. The post Global default for Copilot features generally available appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: Industry comparisons in the Copilot impact dashboard
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: The Copilot impact dashboard now includes an “Industry comparison” section. Enterprises, and organizations that aren’t owned by an enterprise, can compare their Copilot agentic adoption and leverage with aggregated benchmarks from participating peers. Participation is opt-in and disabled by default. What’s new Agentic adoption and leverage benchmarks — See the percentage of your users who are agent-first or multi-agent, and how the pull request merge rate of agentic users compares with nonagentic users. Once enough businesses have opted in, each score is ranked against the peer median for the 28-day reporting period and against the top decile as the peer group grows. Peer groups by company size and industry — Choose a company size (e.g., 1–999, 1,000–4,999, or 5,000+ employees) and one of ten industries, then switch between your industry and all industries. If your industry’s peer group is too small, the comparison widens to all industries for your company size, and the dashboard labels the peer group it used. Copilot metrics industry comparison policy — Opt in from the dashboard or centrally from your enterprise or organization Copilot policies. Both places use the same policy, so turning it off in either place stops both contributing data and seeing comparisons. Why this matters Enterprise leaders can measure their own Copilot adoption, but until now they couldn’t tell whether it was leading or lagging comparable businesses. Industry comparisons add the peer context needed to set realistic goals, identify adoption gaps, and communicate progress. Important notes Rankings appear only after enough businesses have opted in to form a peer group. Especially soon after launch, you might see only the median, a broader peer group than you selected, or no ranking until more peers join. Rankings also aren’t shown when your own score can’t be calculated such as when all your users are already agent-first or multi-agent, leaving no nonagentic baseline for leverage. Comparisons
items.why_it_matters: Copilot's impact dashboard adds opt-in industry benchmarks for agentic adoption and PR merge rates. These could inform how fractional CTOs measure agent productivity for clients.

items.title: Public monitoring now available with data residency
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Public monitoring is now available in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency (GHEC DR). Public monitoring with data residency Public monitoring extends secret scanning beyond internal repositories by monitoring public commits across github.com, attributing exposed credentials back to your enterprise in real time. For enterprises hosted in data residency regions, attribution is powered exclusively by verified domain matching. Because data residency environments maintain strict tenant isolation from github.com, enterprise membership rosters are not shared across the boundary. Instead, when a commit author’s email matches a domain your enterprise has verified, the alert is encrypted and delivered directly to your enterprise dashboard while ensuring data stays within your designated geography. Eligibility and billing Public monitoring is available in public preview for GitHub Enterprise Cloud customers with data residency. Using public monitoring requires an active GitHub Advanced Security or GitHub Secret Protection license. Enterprise admins and enterprise security managers can enable the feature under enterprise security settings. Public monitoring is included with your GitHub Advanced Security or GitHub Secret Protection license at no additional cost. Learn more Learn more about secret scanning and verifying domains for your enterprise, or share your feedback in the community discussion. The post Public monitoring now available with data residency appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: Pull requests: Saved whitespace preferences and improved split view
items.author: Allison
items.excerpt: Two improvements make it easier to review pull requests in the “Files changed” page: You can save your whitespace visibility preference across pull requests New and deleted files now use the full width in split view Save your whitespace visibility preference Open Settings → Whitespace changes and choose Always show, Always hide, or Hide for this diff only. Your saved preference is personal and applies across pull requests. When whitespace is hidden, an active Hide whitespace filter appears beside All commits. Select its X to temporarily show whitespace without changing your saved preference. File counts and diff statistics reflect the displayed diff. Review new and deleted files in split view In split view, new and deleted files now span both columns, as they do in unified view. This gives you more room to review new files and reduces line wrapping. Leave your questions or feedback in our Community discussion. The post Pull requests: Saved whitespace preferences and improved split view appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

items.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
items.author: Shilpa Kumari
items.excerpt: As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n! As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone. The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same. However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists. Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. Learn more about how to qualify on our public bounty site. As we wrap up our Cybersecurity Awareness Month celebration, we interview @r31n, a researcher renowned for their work on GitHub Enterprise Server, where they have repeatedly uncovered high-impact issues. Their reports consistently include working proofs of concept and clear reproduction steps, helping our engineering teams move from triage to remediation more quickly. items.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO
items.author: Basil Chatha
items.excerpt: Warm welcome to Basil Chatha, our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D!Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience.A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate, raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation, and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it.Watch the full conversation on YouTube →GPU demand isn’t rectangularA typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand.Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad: Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices.There is a financial risk on the other side. items.title: Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal
items.author: Latent Space
items.excerpt: AI workloads don’t run in neat, three-year rectangles. But much of the GPU market still sells capacity that way. Modal CEO Erik Bernhardsson joins Latent Space to explain how Modal pools compute, scales AI workloads and thinks about the financial risks of building a GPU cloud. Erik takes us from building Spotify’s recommendation system to founding Modal, then digs into GPU supply, alternative accelerators and the surprising growth of agent sandboxes. We also discuss sandbox security, developer experience in the age of agents, forward-deployed engineers and why Modal makes code review optional.
